opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is to be honest about where the technology actually is, rather than where we wish it were. There's a temptation to go straight for the most impressive demo, like a humanoid that does everything in your home, but the applications that will matter over the next ten years are the ones where three things line up.

First, there has to be real demand: a job people genuinely need done that is dangerous, repetitive, physically exhausting, or simply hard to staff. Elder care support, logistics, agriculture, and certain manufacturing tasks all have big labor gaps. If a robot solves a problem nobody is paying to solve, it stays a research project.

Second, the environment has to be one where the robot can succeed reliably enough. Robots don't need to be perfect, but the tolerance for error depends on the setting. In a warehouse, dropping a box now and then is fine. In a hospital or around a frail person, it's not. So I look for settings that are structured, or can be made structured, and where mistakes are recoverable. That's where you can deploy early, gather data, and improve.

Third, and people underestimate this one, the application has to create a data flywheel. Robot learning is still bottlenecked by real-world physical data. If deploying a robot lets you collect more useful data, which makes the robot better, which lets you deploy more widely, you've found something that can compound. Many applications look good on paper but never produce that loop.

Beyond those three, I'd add one more consideration: how the work feels for the people around the robot. The best applications augment workers and take over the parts of the job people don't want, rather than treating humans as an obstacle. That affects adoption more than most engineers expect.

So my short answer is to start where the need is real, the environment is forgiving, and the data compounds. The general-purpose dream will come, but it will be built on top of many narrower successes like these.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes real demand, forgiving environments, and reliable performance, but it does not identify whether the robot’s intelligence is sufficient for a particular application as the key selection criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the single most important thing is to start from the task, not from the robot. For a long time our field has been technology-driven. We build a humanoid or a dexterous hand and then we go looking for somewhere to use it. Over the next decade I think the winners will flip that around and ask: where is there real, sustained demand for physical work that humans either can't do, don't want to do, or can't do at the scale needed?

So I'd put three criteria at the top.

First, the value of the task has to justify the system cost today, not in some hypothetical future where hardware is ten times cheaper. Logistics, manufacturing, inspection, agriculture, and eldercare support all have very clear labor gaps and very clear economics. If a robot can take over even one repetitive step reliably, a customer will pay for it. Home robots that do everything are exciting, but the gap between a demo and something that runs every day in a messy apartment is still large.

Second, the environment has to be structured enough that you can reach high reliability. Intelligence in robots is improving fast, especially with foundation models, but a model that succeeds ninety percent of the time is useless in a factory and dangerous in a hospital. I prefer applications where the robot can start in a semi-structured setting, collect data, and gradually expand its envelope. That data flywheel is really what matters. The application you choose determines what data you collect, and the data determines how fast the intelligence grows.

Third, I look at safety and trust. Any application that puts a robot next to people has to earn acceptance slowly. So I'd rather pick tasks where failure modes are benign and recoverable, and build a track record there, before moving to higher-stakes scenarios.

If I had to summarize it in one sentence: pick a problem that is painful enough that people need it solved, bounded enough that the robot can actually be reliable, and rich enough in data that each deployment makes the next one smarter. If you have those three things, the technology will catch up to you. If you don't, no amount of impressive hardware will save the business.

r001.rationale: The response says application choice should account for whether robot intelligence can achieve useful reliability in that setting, noting that 90% success is inadequate in factories or hospitals and favoring tasks where the robot can be reliable.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is to start with a real need. What task do people actually want a robot to do, and why isn’t that task being done well today? Maybe it’s dangerous, physically demanding, or something where there simply aren’t enough people available.

Then you have to ask whether the robot can deliver value reliably. A successful demo is very different from a machine that works every day, with reasonable costs for maintenance, supervision, and recovery when something goes wrong. You have to look at the whole system, not just how intelligent the robot appears to be.

Over the next decade, I would favor applications with a clear task, a manageable environment, and enough repetition to learn from deployment. You can expand from there. The best application isn’t necessarily the most impressive thing a robot can do—it’s something useful that people will keep using.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes real needs, reliability, costs, and deployment conditions. It does not identify whether the robot’s intelligence is sufficient for a particular application as the key selection criterion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is to start with a real need. What problem are we solving, and does a robot actually make the solution better? A task can be technically impressive without being useful enough for someone to pay for it.

I would look for applications where the work is repetitive, physically demanding, or dangerous, and where success can be measured clearly. Then you have to consider the whole deployment: reliability, safety, maintenance, and how the robot fits into the way people already work.

Over the next decade, I think the strongest applications will be ones where robots can deliver value with the capabilities they have today, while improving through experience. You need a useful starting point and a practical path to expand from there.

r001.rationale: The response says to choose applications where robots can deliver value with their current capabilities, but it does not clearly identify whether the robot’s intelligence is sufficient for a specific application as the key criterion.
